questions.scenario: VM1 runs Windows Server and is currently running. In the Size blade, the size Standard_E8s_v5 is unavailable for selection.
questions.question: What should you do first so that you can resize VM1 to Standard_E8s_v5?

options.text: Stop (deallocate) VM1
options.why: Correct. Deallocating releases VM1 from its hardware cluster so that every size in the region becomes available.

options.text: Restart VM1
options.why: A restart keeps the VM on the same hardware cluster.

options.text: Shut down VM1 from inside the operating system
options.why: This leaves VM1 allocated to the same cluster.

options.text: Detach the data disks of VM1
options.why: Disks are not the reason a size is unavailable on the current cluster.

questions.explanation: Sizes that are not available on the current cluster can be selected after the VM is deallocated.

questions.question: You resize a running virtual machine from Standard_D2s_v5 to Standard_D4s_v5. The new size is available on the current hardware cluster. What is the effect on the virtual machine?

options.text: The virtual machine restarts
options.why: Correct. A resize always restarts the VM.

options.text: The virtual machine is resized with no interruption
options.why: Resizing requires a restart.

options.text: The virtual machine is deleted and recreated with new disks
options.why: The disks and configuration are kept.

options.text: The temporary disk is converted to a managed disk
options.why: Resizing does not change the type of the temporary disk.

questions.explanation: Plan a resize in a maintenance window because it causes a short outage.

questions.scenario: A line-of-business application runs an in-memory database that needs a high memory-to-vCPU ratio. You need to choose a VM size family.
questions.question: Which family should you choose?

options.text: E-series
options.why: Correct. E-series sizes are memory optimised.

options.text: F-series
options.why: F-series sizes are compute optimised with a low memory-to-vCPU ratio.

options.text: B-series
options.why: B-series sizes are burstable and suit mostly idle workloads.

options.text: N-series
options.why: N-series sizes provide GPUs.

questions.explanation: D is general purpose, E is memory optimised, F is compute optimised, L is storage optimised and N is GPU.

questions.question: You need to create a Linux virtual machine in availability zone 2 by using the Azure CLI. Which command should you run?

options.text: az vm create --resource-group RG1 --name VM1 --image Ubuntu2404 --zone 2 --generate-ssh-keys
options.why: Correct. --zone places the VM in the specified availability zone.

options.text: az vm create --resource-group RG1 --name VM1 --image Ubuntu2404 --availability-set 2
options.why: --availability-set expects the name of an availability set, not a zone.

options.text: az vm create --resource-group RG1 --name VM1 --image Ubuntu2404 --location zone2
options.why: zone2 is not a location. Zones are selected with --zone.

options.text: az vmss create --resource-group RG1 --name VM1 --image Ubuntu2404 --instance-count 2
options.why: This creates a scale set with two instances.

questions.explanation: In PowerShell, use New-AzVM with the -Zone parameter.

questions.scenario: VM1 is not used outside business hours. Compute charges for VM1 must stop overnight while its disks and configuration are kept.
questions.question: What should you do each evening?

options.text: Stop VM1 from the Azure portal so that it is deallocated
options.why: Correct. A deallocated VM is not billed for compute. Disks remain and are still billed.

options.text: Shut down VM1 from inside the operating system
options.why: The VM stays allocated and compute is still billed.

options.text: Resize VM1 to Standard_B1s
options.why: A smaller size still incurs compute charges while running.

options.text: Delete VM1 and keep the OS disk
options.why: This removes the VM configuration, which must be kept.

questions.explanation: Stopped (deallocated) ends compute billing. Stopped (allocated) does not.
